newsitem.title: USA: Glickman-US may subsidize wheat flour, malt exports.
newsitem.headline: Glickman-US may subsidize wheat flour, malt exports.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman confirmed Tuesday that the United States is considering renewing export subsidies for wheat flour and barley malt.
But, in remarks to the Commodity Club, Glickman noted that market conditions did not yet justify renewing export subsidies for wheat and other bulk commodities.

On a separate subject, Glickman repeated that the United States would not tolerate any requirements that genetically modified crops be segregated from non-modified crops. Consumer concerns in the European Union over the safety of genetically modified crops raised the prospect that officials there might require such segregation.
However, such a move would effectively block billions of dollars of U.S. agricultural exports since genetically modified corn and soybeans are routinely mixed with their unmodified counterparts.
Should the EU impose such a requirement, the U.S. would use all its options including going to the World Trade Organization to have the requirement removed, Glickman said.

Glickman told reporters that the issue of again subsidizing wheat flour and barley exports has been raised in recent discussions between USDA and other agencies that have a voice in the operation of the Export Enhancement Program.
"I've indicated a concern about wheat flour and barley malt" because of the sharp drop in U.S. exports of those commodities in recent years, Glickman said.
However, it is still "very premature" to talk about reviving export subsidies for wheat and other bulk commodities given current market conditions, he said.

On a related note, Glickman said USDA "could probably live with" a $270 million cap that House appropriators have put on EEP for fiscal 1998. "I prefer to see it higher," but appropriators had to make a trade-off to fund other important agriculture programs, he said.
Glickman also noted that USDA could always request more EEP funds in fiscal 1998 if it needs them.
